intro.html: When feelings run hot, these are the words for cooling them down. Some comfort a person who is hurting; some win over a person who is angry, often by giving something; some shrink a bad feeling; one stops trouble outright; and two settle a quarrel.

Comfort: soothe, console. Win over someone angry: appease, mollify, conciliate. Ease a feeling: assuage (pain, hunger, guilt), allay (fear, worry, doubt). Stop it: quell. Settle a conflict: reconcile, defuse.

words.def: to calm or comfort, often gently; to ease pain
words.ex: Priya hummed an old lullaby to {soothe} the fussy baby.
words.ctx: Lila had tossed and turned for an hour, but the steady patter of rain on the roof {soothed} her, and soon her worries about the test faded into sleep.

mn.text: Priya sings a smooth, slow lullaby, and little Theo’s crying fades into sleepy sighs. Her song {soothes} him.

scene.alt: A mother sings softly beside her toddler, who drifts off to sleep in bed.

words.def: to comfort someone who is sad or disappointed
words.ex: Rosa {consoled} her little brother after his kite blew away.
words.ctx: Losing the spelling bee by a single letter crushed Dev, so his grandmother {consoled} him with a hug and a reminder of how far he had come since last year.
words.etym: From Latin consolari, “to comfort”: con (with) + solari (to comfort), the root of solace.
words.note: The noun CON-sole (a cabinet or a control panel) is a different word with the stress on the first syllable.

mn.cue: a CONE for a SAD SOUL
mn.text: Pip comes in last in the race, so Nana Lou hands him an ice cream cone and a hug: “You ran your best.” She {consoles} him.

scene.alt: A grandmother offers an ice cream cone and kind words to a tearful boy who lost a race.

words.def: to calm someone by giving them what they demand
words.ex: To stop the twins’ chant of “Snacks! Snacks!”, Mom {appeased} them with a plate of crackers.
words.ctx: The king tried to {appease} the angry dragon with a cartload of gold, hoping that once it got what it wanted, it would leave the village in peace.
words.etym: From Old French apaisier, “to bring to peace”: a (to) + pais (peace), from Latin pax.
words.note: Appease can carry a warning: giving in to demands may buy calm now but invite bigger demands later.

mn.text: The dragon roars for its dinner, so Sven slides it a giant bowl of peas. Full and happy, it settles down: Sven {appeases} the dragon.

scene.alt: A nervous man offers a big bowl of peas to a dragon, which calms down happily.

words.ex: A free dessert {mollified} the diner whose soup had come out cold.
words.ctx: The neighbor was furious about the broken window until the boys offered to pay for it from their savings; the offer {mollified} him, and he even helped them find the ball.
words.etym: From Late Latin mollificare, “to make soft”: mollis (soft) + facere (to make).

mn.text: Grandpa Gus is grumbling until little Molly brings him a warm cookie and a hug. His anger softens: Molly {mollifies} him.

scene.alt: A little girl named Molly gives her grandfather a cookie, and his grumpy face softens into a smile.

words.def: to make a bad feeling, such as hunger, pain or guilt, less strong
words.ex: A tall glass of lemonade {assuaged} our thirst after the long hike.
words.ctx: Nothing could fully {assuage} Ada’s guilt about forgetting her best friend’s birthday, but the handmade card she sent the next morning helped a little.
words.etym: From Old French assouagier, from Latin ad (to) + suavis (sweet, pleasant): to sweeten a bitter feeling.

mn.cue: A SAUSAGE to ASSUAGE his hunger
mn.text: After a long day of hiking, Jamal’s stomach growls. One hot sausage from the campfire {assuages} his hunger.

scene.alt: A hungry camper happily cooks a sausage in a pan over the campfire.

words.def: to make fear, worry or doubt less strong
words.ex: The pilot’s calm voice {allayed} the nervous passengers’ fears.
words.ctx: Parents worried about the new playground, so the builders {allayed} their concerns by showing them the soft ground, the rounded corners and the safety report.
words.etym: From Old English alecgan, “to lay down, to put aside.”
words.note: You allay fears, worries and doubts. Don’t confuse it with alley (a narrow lane) or ally (a friend on your side).

mn.text: Before his checkup, Sami is scared, so Nurse Tia shows him each tool and lets him listen to his own heartbeat. Her kindness {allays} his fears.

scene.alt: A kind nurse explains her tools to a boy sitting on a hospital bed, and his worry fades.

words.def: to put an end to something, such as a riot or a rumor, often by force
words.ex: The teacher {quelled} the giggling with a single raised eyebrow.
words.ctx: A rumor spread that the fair had been canceled, but the organizers quickly {quelled} it by posting photos of the rides already being set up.

mn.text: The lunchroom roars with yelling until Coach Omar blows one sharp whistle, and the noise stops at once. He {quells} the yell.

scene.alt: A coach blows a whistle, and two noisy children instantly fall silent.

words.def: to win over someone who is angry, often by friendly acts
words.ex: The hotel {conciliated} the upset guests with a free night’s stay.
words.ctx: Instead of arguing back, the new manager tried to {conciliate} the angry workers: she listened to every complaint and had the broken heater fixed that same day.
words.etym: From Latin conciliare, “to bring together, to win over,” from concilium, “a meeting,” the source of council.

mn.cue: CON-SILLY-ate: win him over with something SILLY
mn.text: Victor is angry about the ball in his garden, so Greta brings him a pie and sings a silly sorry song. His frown melts: she {conciliates} him.

scene.alt: A woman brings a pie and a silly apology song to her annoyed neighbor, whose frown begins to fade.

words.def: to become friends again after a quarrel; also, to make two things agree
words.ex: After a week of silence, the two friends finally {reconciled} over a shared pizza.
words.ctx: The two stories of the accident seemed impossible to {reconcile}: one driver said the light was green, the other swore it was red, and both had witnesses.
words.etym: From Latin reconciliare, “to bring together again”: re (again) + conciliare (to bring together).

mn.text: Lila and Maya had a wreck of a fight, but now they hug and smile, friends again: they {reconcile}.

scene.alt: Two girls who had quarreled hug and smile, friends again.

words.def: to calm a tense or dangerous situation
words.ex: Pip {defused} the argument at the dinner table by making everyone laugh.
words.ctx: Tempers were rising at the neighborhood meeting until a calm voice {defused} the situation; she suggested a short break, and everyone came back ready to listen.

roots.means: the wick that sets something off

words.etym: From de- (remove) + fuse: first, to take the fuse out of a bomb so it cannot go off; then, to calm a situation before it explodes.
words.note: Defuse (calm a situation) is not diffuse (spread out).

mn.cue: DE-FUSE: put out the FUSE before the BOOM
mn.text: Kai and Dev are about to blow up at each other. Ada pours water on the sizzling fuse of their fight: she {defuses} it.

scene.alt: A calm woman pours water on a sizzling cartoon fuse between two angry boys.

after.cap: Ten ways to cool things down.

after.html: Three look-alikes to keep apart. You defuse a tense situation (as if pulling the fuse from a bomb), but light, smells and ideas diffuse, or spread out. You allay fears; an alley is a lane and an ally is a friend on your side. And appease sometimes carries a warning: giving in to demands can buy calm now and invite bigger demands later.

opts.s: The coach’s calm pep talk {allayed} the team’s fears before the championship game.

items.q: The teacher ______ the argument by asking each student to explain one good point the other had made. Which word fits?
items.why: To defuse is to calm a tense situation, like an argument. Diffuse means to spread out; assuage and allay ease feelings such as hunger or fear.

items.q: True or false: you can allay someone’s fears.
items.why: True. To allay is to lessen fear, worry or doubt. (An alley is a lane; an ally is a friend on your side.)

items.q: After months of not speaking, the two neighbors shook hands and agreed to share the cost of the fence. They…
items.why: Becoming friendly again after a quarrel is reconciling.

items.q: Mollify comes from Latin mollis, which means…
items.why: Mollis means soft: to mollify is to soften someone’s anger.

items.q: Type the verb that means to calm someone by giving them what they demand.
items.why: To appease is to quiet someone’s demands by giving in to them.
